terms.grammar: noun phrase: cīvitās, cīvitātis f., with the adjective populāris
terms.comment: Cicero’s name for the state in which all power lies with the people, beside rule by a king (rēgnum) and by the best men (optimātēs); Pliny sets it against rēgia cīvitās, monarchy. Democratic is populāris (Lewis & Short). Levi and Bini (p. 21) add ratiō populāris for the system and lībera rēs pūblica for democracy in its better sense.

evidence: Serv. ad Aen. 1.21 (M-O s.v. form: democracy)
terms.comment: Greek δημοκρατία. Not in Lewis & Short; Morgan–Owens cites Servius and Dante, and Traupman gives it.

phrases.latin: illa autem est cīvitās populāris (sīc enim appellant), in quā in populō sunt omnia
phrases.english: and that is a democracy, as they call it, in which everything is in the hands of the people

phrases.latin: rēgiam cīvitātem Aegyptiī, populārem Atticī post Thēseum
phrases.english: the Egyptians (invented) monarchy; the Athenians, after Theseus, democracy

sources: Lewis & Short: civitas · Lewis & Short: popularis. Lewis & Short has no entry for dēmocratia.
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. form: democracy.
